snip.t: A 45‑year‑old woman with known macroadenoma presents with sudden severe headache, vomiting and left‑sided ptosis.
CN III palsy may cause ptosis and a dilated pupil, depending on the cause.
Pattern of weakness: Ptosis, diplopia, difficulty chewing, swallowing, speaking, neck flexion, proximal limb weakness, respiratory effort.
Ptosis & variable diplopia – intermittent because extra‑ocular muscles fatigue quickly.
Horner syndrome: ptosis and a small pupil on one side may be relevant in selected apical lung lesions, but requires proper assessment.

qs.q: A 40-year-old man presents with ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, slurred speech, and progressive dysphagia 3 hours after a snake bite in a rural area. Which snake family is most likely responsible for these descending paralytic signs?
o: Viperidae
Elapidae
Atractaspididae
Colubridae
qs.e: Elapidae (such as cobras and mambas) produce neurotoxic venom leading to descending paralysis. Viperidae venoms are primarily haemotoxic and cytotoxic.
qs.s: Skin and Soft Tissue Infections, and Snake Bites: MCQs

qs.q: A 50-year-old female presents with a severe thunderclap headache and is found to have a complete left-sided third cranial nerve palsy, including a dilated, unreactive pupil and ptosis, along with retro-orbital pain. Which specific aneurysm site is most consistent with this localising sign?
o: Middle cerebral artery
Basilar artery tip
Posterior communicating artery
Anterior communicating artery
qs.e: An aneurysm at the internal carotid or posterior communicating artery can cause compression of the third cranial nerve, leading to ipsilateral ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, and a dilated pupil. Other locations present with different focal deficits such as aphasia or bilateral leg weakness.
qs.s: Subarachnoid Haemorrhage and Intracranial Aneurysms: MCQs

qs.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with fluctuating muscle weakness, diplopia, and ptosis that worsens with exertion. Anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies are detected. What is the frequency of associated thymic abnormalities in this condition?
o: Thymic hyperplasia in about 30% and thymoma in 10%
Thymic hyperplasia in about 80% and thymoma in 50%
Thymic hyperplasia in about 10% and thymoma in 30%
Thymic hyperplasia in about 50% and thymoma in 80%
qs.e: Myasthenia gravis is associated with thymic hyperplasia in about 30 percent of patients (especially younger ones) and thymoma in about 10 percent. Thymic abnormalities are not universal or entirely absent as implied by the incorrect options.
qs.s: Pathology of Demyelinating Diseases: MS, NMO, ADEM, CPM: MCQs

qs.q: A patient has diplopia, poor accommodation, absent direct and consensual light reflexes, and ptosis. Which statement is true? ---
o: Oculomotor nerve supplies the superior levator palpebrae
Horner's syndrome should be considered as primary diagnosis
A cerebellar lesion is most likely causing these symptoms
Trigeminal nerve supplies motor fibres to the frontalis
qs.e: The oculomotor nerve innervates the levator palpebrae superioris, and its palsy causes ptosis, diplopia, and pupil changes.
qs.s: MBChB Clinical Exam: Cranial Nerves, Resp & Abdominal Skills

qs.q: On drooping of the eyelid (ptosis), which statement is FALSE? ---
o: It can be congenital or acquired in origin
It can be due to injury or stretching of muscles
It has been associated with apical lung tumors
It is never associated with Myasthenia gravis
qs.e: Myasthenia gravis is a well-known cause of ptosis, making the statement that it is not associated false.
qs.s: MBChB Clinical Exam: Cranial Nerves, Resp & Abdominal Skills

qs.q: A 58-year-old male with a right apical lung mass develops right-sided ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis, enophthalmos, and severe pain radiating down the ulnar aspect of the right arm. CT shows rib destruction. The complete diagnosis is
o: Paraneoplastic autonomic neuropathy arising from small cell lung carcinoma
Superior vena cava syndrome resulting from mediastinal lymph node compression
Pancoast tumour causing Pancoast syndrome including classic Horner syndrome
Isolated Horner syndrome resulting from direct sympathetic chain involvement
qs.e: An apical lung tumour invading the brachial and cervical sympathetic plexus causes Pancoast syndrome — Horner syndrome plus ulnar nerve pain and rib destruction are collectively termed Pancoast syndrome.
